planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this selection is grown specifically for having the strongest, most far-carrying scent of any tea olive in cultivation.

directions: Fragrantissimus is a vigorous, large-growing tea olive selection singled out from seedling populations for producing an unusually intense, carrying fragrance even by the standards of an already famously perfumed species. It builds into a broad, dense, multi-stemmed evergreen faster than typical seed-grown sweet olive, making it a good choice for a big screening hedge or specimen where its scale won't be a problem. Bloom is heaviest in fall with lighter repeat flushes into spring and, in the mildest zones, sporadically through winter. Because it is somewhat more cold-sensitive than compact cultivars like Fudingzhu, site it with some wind protection near the northern edge of its range and expect occasional dieback after hard freezes there.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this botanical form is distinguished from typical tea olive mainly by its noticeably wider, coarser-toothed leaves.

directions: The latifolius form of fragrant tea olive is grown for its broader, more heavily serrated leaves, which give the shrub a coarser, bolder texture than the narrow, smooth-edged foliage typical of the species. Flower size, color, and the intense sweet apricot fragrance are essentially unchanged from standard sweet olive, so it is chosen mainly by collectors and gardeners wanting a textural variation on a familiar Gulf South favorite. It responds well to the same culture as other tea olive forms, tolerating light shearing if used as a screen or informal hedge. Give it protection from harsh winter wind at the cold edge of its range, since leaf and stem damage can occur below the mid-teens Fahrenheit.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; Yatsubusa is a compact, slow-growing sansho selection bred for container culture and small-space kitchen gardens.

directions: Yatsubusa is a naturally dwarf, densely branched selection of Japanese sansho pepper that tops out at only a few feet tall, in contrast to the much larger habit of standard sansho, while still producing the same aromatic kinome leaves and numbing, citrusy green peppercorns used in Japanese cooking. Its small stature and slow growth rate make it well suited to a large patio container or a compact bed near the kitchen, where both male and female plants should be grown together if a berry harvest is wanted alongside the leaf crop. Give it some afternoon shade and steady moisture, since the shallow root system in a pot dries out faster than an in-ground shrub. Prune lightly to maintain shape rather than to control size, since this cultivar is naturally restrained compared to its parent species.
sources: Japan Times — Sansho and Kinome Culinary Guide

planting.note: Plant container stock after all frost danger has passed in humus-rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in partial shade, mimicking the cool tropical highland understory this species grows in on Sumatra.

directions: Andaliman is the signature spice of Batak cuisine from the highlands of North Sumatra, prized for its bright, citrusy aroma and the same tongue-numbing sanshool compounds found in Sichuan pepper, but with a fresher, more limey character than its Chinese relatives. Unripe green berries are harvested and used fresh or dried, most famously in the fish and pork dishes arsik and saksang. Because it naturally grows as an understory shrub in cool, humid highland forest, it prefers filtered light and consistently moist, rich soil rather than full sun and is intolerant of any frost, limiting outdoor culture to the warmest, nearly frost-free gardens or large containers overwintered under cover elsewhere. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, so more than one specimen is needed for a fruit harvest.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

common_name: Indian Prickly Ash (Triphal, Konkani Pepper Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown saplings after frost danger has passed in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing generous room since this species grows into a substantial tree over time.

directions: Zanthoxylum rhetsa is a large, thorny tree of South and Southeast Asia whose dried, split seed capsules are sold as triphal, a key spice in Konkani and Maharashtrian coastal cuisine used to flavor fish curries, pickles, and lentil dishes with the same tingling, numbing sensation found in Sichuan pepper. The bark and fruit are also used in traditional Ayurvedic preparations. It needs a long, warm growing season and considerable overhead and root room to reach fruiting size, making it a tree for spacious, essentially frost-free landscapes rather than a typical garden shrub border. Harvest the ripening capsules once they begin to split and dry them further indoors before storing in an airtight container for spice use.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
